 {"list":[{"chapter_code":"JDG07","exceeding":[{"verses":"23","findings":[{"word":"מִדְיָֽן׃","parsing":"Noun - proper - masculine singular","term":"perfect","elsewhere":[],"explain":"The name Midian, masculine and one of him. The Midianites. And Midian for the seventh time in the chapter, and this is the first standing of the name that is not attached to a camp or a hand. The camp of Midian, verse one. The camp of Midian, verse eight. Midian and Amalek, verse twelve. The camp of Midian, verse thirteen. Midian into his hand, verse fourteen. The camp of Midian, verse fifteen. And now just Midian, running, with Israel behind him. Ten things worth carrying out of this verse. First, and worth carrying hardest of all: these are the men who were sent home. Count them. Verse three sent twenty-two thousand away. Verse eight sent the remaining nine thousand seven hundred to their tents. Thirty-one thousand seven hundred men were deliberately kept out of this fight so that nobody could say mine own hand hath saved me — and the moment the fight is over, here they come. Out of Naphtali, out of Asher, out of all Manasseh, chasing. God would not let them win it. He is perfectly willing to let them finish it. There is a whole doctrine of work in that, and the text states it as a fact and moves on. Second, and worth carrying hardest too: the crying-out word is where this entire story began. Chapter six opens with Israel crying out to the LORD because of Midian — that is the twin of this verb, and Hebrew has two crying-out words spelled with different first letters and uses them almost interchangeably. Here the same crying is turned round the other way. Israel cried out because of Midian; now Israel is cried out against Midian. The shout that started the book as a complaint ends the battle as a muster. Third, and worth carrying: the man of Israel is the enemy's own phrase. In verse fourteen a frightened Midianite said this is nothing else save the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel. Two Hebrew words. Here the writer uses those same two words for the entire nation coming out to chase. The enemy's description of one man has become the writer's description of everybody. Fourth, the tribes in this list were already on a list once. In chapter six Gideon blew a horn and sent messengers, and they went to Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali. Three of those four names stand here. Zebulun is missing and the writer says nothing about why, so neither will I. What he does say is that the people Gideon called at the start are the people who answer at the end. Fifth, Manasseh is Gideon's own tribe, and he had opinions about it. When the angel called him a mighty man of valour he answered: my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. The tribe he called poor turns out in full — all Manasseh — and the man who called himself the least of it is the reason they are out on the road. Sixth, the all-word turns up again, and it is worth seeing the whole journey it has made. It has meant the army about to be gutted, the men going home, all the sons of the east, all the camp of the enemy twice over, all who are with me, every last one of the three hundred who got a horn, and all the camp where the swords turned. Here, finally, it means a tribe of Israel arriving in full strength. Seventh, the writer changes the number of his verbs inside one sentence and means it. The being-called-out is in the shape for one person, because Hebrew says the man of Israel. The chasing is in the shape for many, because by then there are thousands on the road. One shout goes out to one Israel; a crowd comes back. Eighth, this is the first chasing in the chapter, and it comes after the fighting is finished. Twenty-two verses of subtracting, waiting, creeping, standing still — and the very first time anybody in Judges seven moves toward the enemy, there is nothing left to move toward but a back. Ninth, the little after-word says more than it looks like saying. They are not fighting Midian; they are behind him. You cannot chase a man who is standing his ground. That one word reports the whole state of the enemy without describing it, and the writer trusts you to notice. Tenth, this is the first time Midian is named without a camp or a hand attached. Six times already in this chapter: the camp of Midian, the camp of Midian, Midian and Amalek, the camp of Midian, Midian into his hand, the camp of Midian. Here he is simply Midian, with no camp left to belong to and nobody's hand to be given into, and Israel is behind him on the road. The mark at the end closes the verse."}]}]}],"json":{"hint":"original_bible: 1 of 478 authored chapters explain a word by naming a form no word of its passage carries - swap the wording in each with app_original_bible_gloss_chapter_explains_text_replace, which takes the chapter code and finds the file itself"}}
